title: Migration Strategies: The 7 Rs & Migration Tooling

scenes.narration: Chapter eighteen opens the migration domain of the AWS certified solutions architect Professional exam — S A P dash C zero two — a domain that carries a real twenty percent weight, tied for the second largest of the exam's four domains. It's a domain almost entirely about judgment: given a company's stated constraints — a deadline, a budget, a skill gap, a licensing headache — pick the migration strategy, one of exactly seven, and the AWS service that actually executes it. The exam expects you to know all seven by name, not just the popular three, and its favorite trap is picking the fanciest one when the scenario's own stated constraint demands something faster.

scenes.narration: Here's the instinct almost every technically strong candidate walks in with. Of the seven migration strategies, refactor, or re-architect, produces the most cloud-native end state — serverless instead of always-on servers, managed databases instead of self-managed instances, event-driven microservices instead of a monolith. So when a scenario describes a company migrating to AWS, the reflex is to reach for the fanciest transformation available and present it as the obviously correct answer. A typical scenario reads: a company's data-center lease expires in ninety days, they run four hundred servers as a monolith, and they want to modernize while migrating. The candidate who's internalized 'cloud native is always better' picks a full refactor — and it reads like the most senior-sounding choice on the page.

props.heading: "Obviously we should refactor — it's the best long-term outcome"
bullets: Refactor produces the most cloud-native, most elastic, most cost-optimized end state of all seven strategies.
So the reflex is: any migration scenario is a chance to reach for the fanciest transformation available.
A scenario states a 90-day data-center lease and a wish to "modernize while migrating" — and the trap is set.

scenes.narration: Refactoring four hundred servers' worth of monolithic logic into microservices isn't a lift, it's a redesign — re-architecting data models, rewriting business logic, building new observability, and running dual operation while it's validated. That's realistically a multi-quarter-to-multi-year program, and the scenario gave you ninety days. On time: rehost can move hundreds of servers in weeks using continuous block-level replication, while refactor needs a redesign cycle measured in months to years. On skill: rehost needs an agent install and a validated test launch, while refactor needs application architects and a team that can safely run the new design. On risk: a stalled refactor leaves you running two systems in parallel indefinitely, directly threatening a hard deadline like a lease expiration. A design that cannot fit inside the stated constraint is not a more ambitious correct answer on this exam — it's simply wrong, no matter how technically superior the end state would be.

props.heading: Refactor is the slowest, highest-skill, highest-cost R by construction
steps: Time: Rehost moves hundreds of servers in weeks via continuous replication — Refactor needs a redesign measured in months to years
Skill: Rehost needs an agent install and a test launch — Refactor needs application architects and new operational tooling
Risk: a stalled Refactor means running two systems in parallel indefinitely — worse than the original problem
A design that can't fit inside the stated constraint isn't a more ambitious correct answer — it's a wrong answer, full stop

scenes.narration: There are exactly seven migration strategies in the real framework AWS uses. Retire: decommission a workload nobody needs anymore — no destination exists. Retain: keep it exactly where it is for now, often for a compliance or hardware reason — not a failure state. Rehost: move it as-is, lift and shift, the fastest strategy. Replatform: lift and reshape, some optimization, most often a database moving onto a managed engine. Repurchase: drop and shop, switching to a different product entirely, often a SaaS replacement. Refactor, or re-architect: redesign for cloud native, the slowest and highest-payoff of the seven. And Relocate: move an entire virtualized environment, hypervisor included, without touching the guest operating system or app inside it — distinct from rehost, which changes what the operating system sits on.

props.heading: The 7 Rs, in the order the exam expects
steps: Retire — decommission it, nobody needs it anymore
Retain — keep it exactly where it is, for now
Rehost — move it as-is, "lift and shift"
Replatform — move it with some optimization, "lift and reshape"
Relocate — move the whole virtualized environment, hypervisor and all

scenes.narration: Five tools map to this framework, and the exam's favorite wrong-answer pairing is mixing them up. Application Migration Service — say the letters, M G N — executes rehost: install a lightweight agent, replicate continuously, then cut over with a short downtime window. Database Migration Service, D M S, executes replatform and straight database migrations — it moves and replicates data. When source and target run different database engines, that's a heterogeneous migration, and DMS alone isn't enough: the Schema Conversion Tool, S C T, runs first to convert schema and stored procedures. And Migration Hub is a tracking and aggregation layer only — it pulls status from Discovery, MGN, and DMS onto one dashboard, but it has no idea how to move a server or a database by itself. Proposing Migration Hub as the tool that performs a migration is one of the most common wrong answers in this domain.

props.heading: 5 tools, mapped to the strategies they actually execute

rows.label: Application Discovery Service
cells: Inventories on-prem servers and dependencies before any wave is planned

rows.label: Application Migration Service (MGN)
cells: Agent-based continuous block-level replication, test launch, then a short cutover

rows.label: Database Migration Service (DMS)
cells: Moves and replicates data — homogeneous engines need nothing else

rows.label: Schema Conversion Tool (SCT)
cells: Converts schema/procedures ahead of DMS when source and target engines differ

rows.label: Migration Hub
cells: Aggregates status from Discovery, MGN and DMS across a multi-wave program

scenes.narration: Picture that qualitative comparison as two opposing scales, each strategy scored zero to a hundred. On migration speed, rehost and relocate sit near the top — both move fast because neither touches the application itself. Refactor sits at the bottom, the slowest by construction. Flip to cloud-native benefit realized and the ranking inverts: refactor scores highest, rehost and relocate lowest, and replatform sits in the middle on both scales. This is the shape the exam is really testing — whichever R buys you the most cloud-native benefit is, by construction, the one that costs you the most time and skill to get there.

props.heading: Migration speed vs. cloud-native benefit realized

scenes.narration: Here's the trap dressed up as a real scenario. Northfield Freight runs three hundred eighty servers across two colocation racks, running a monolithic dispatch and routing application. Their colocation contract expires in a hundred days and won't be renewed at any price the business will accept. There's executive appetite to modernize while migrating, but zero appetite for missing that exit date. The trap answer reaches for the fanciest option on the page: a full refactor into microservices, because it reads like the most senior recommendation. The correct read is the opposite — a hundred days is a hard, numeric, stated constraint, and a redesign of that fleet cannot be safely completed and cut over in that window. The right call is rehost via MGN now: the replication agent goes on every server, initial sync runs continuously in the background, test launches validate the cutover, and the whole fleet exits inside the hundred-day window. Refactor candidates get identified and scheduled afterward, as a second, unhurried phase. Constraint, then R, then tool — never the reverse.

props.heading: A fancier R is not a better answer than the constraint allows
bullets: Northfield Freight: 380 servers, a colocation lease expiring in 100 days, and executive appetite to "modernize while we're at it"
The trap answer: propose a full Refactor into microservices because it's the most sophisticated-sounding option on the page
The correct read: 100 days is a hard, numeric, non-negotiable constraint that a redesign cannot fit inside
Correct call: Rehost via MGN now — hit the deadline safely, schedule Refactor candidates as an unhurried second phase afterward

scenes.narration: Four commands trace the shape of a real rehost wave. Describing source servers confirms replication state — by cutover day, most of the data volume already synced continuously in the background, which is exactly why the actual downtime window stays short. Starting a test launches a fully isolated, non-disruptive instance from that replicated data, so the team validates the cutover before touching production traffic — the exam loves testing whether you know this rehearsal step exists. Starting the cutover kicks off the real switch: only the final delta needs to catch up, not the whole server from scratch. And finalizing the cutover closes it out, clearing the way to decommission the source. Recognizing this order — test before cutover, and that most of the sync work already happened before cutover day — is the actual skill being tested, not memorizing flag syntax.

props.heading: MGN rehost commands, start to cutover

output: # most data already synced well before cutover day
Test instance launching in an isolated network...
# fully isolated — doesn't touch production traffic
Cutover started — syncing final delta only
# most of the data moved days ago, continuously
# source server can now be decommissioned

scenes.narration: One representative layout shows how a migration wave's tooling actually divides the work. Discovery holds Application Discovery Service's server inventory and dependency maps — the input every other decision gets planned from. Rehost holds MGN's launch template and per-server agent install logs. Replatform holds the Schema Conversion Tool's automated-versus-manual conversion report, plus DMS's replication task definitions — table mappings and transformation rules. And tracking holds one roll-up file that Migration Hub maintains across every server and database in the wave, which is exactly why Migration Hub sits outside the rehost and replatform folders — it isn't a peer execution step, it spans all of them.

props.kicker: WHAT A MIGRATION WAVE ACTUALLY PRODUCES

lines: └── migration-hub-waves.csv    # rolled up across every wave

scenes.narration: Take a concrete case. Meridian Claims runs a large self-managed commercial database on EC2 whose annual license renewal has become the single largest line item in their infrastructure budget. They want off that license and onto a managed engine, but the application's SQL and stored procedures are deeply tied to the current engine's dialect, and a full rewrite isn't funded. Run it through the framework: the destination engine differs from the source, so this is a heterogeneous migration. The correct call is replatform via DMS plus the Schema Conversion Tool — SCT converts the schema and as much procedural logic as it safely can up front, DMS handles the ongoing data replication and cutover, and the license cost and patching burden disappear without funding a rewrite nobody budgeted for.

props.heading: The license renewal nobody wants to sign again

profile.verdict: Replatform via DMS + SCT: SCT converts schema and as much procedural logic as it safely can; DMS handles ongoing replication and cutover; the license cost disappears without a full rewrite.

scenes.narration: Try these before we reveal the answers. First: a company has sixty days before their data-center lease ends, and five hundred servers to move. A colleague wants to use the migration as a chance to fully re-architect into microservices. What should you recommend instead? Second: you're replatforming a self-managed database onto a different, non-matching managed engine using Database Migration Service. What else does this heterogeneous migration require, and why?

questions.prompt: A company has 60 days before its data-center lease ends and 500 servers to move. A colleague wants to use the migration as a chance to fully re-architect into microservices. What should you recommend instead?
options: Proceed with the full microservice refactor — it delivers the most cloud-native benefit
Rehost via Application Migration Service now; schedule refactor work for specific components after the move completes
Retain the workload on-premises until the refactor is finished
Repurchase a SaaS product that replaces all 500 servers' functionality

questions.prompt: You're replatforming a self-managed database to a different, non-matching managed engine using Database Migration Service. What else does this heterogeneous migration require, and why?
options: Nothing else — DMS converts schema and stored procedures automatically during replication
Application Migration Service, to replicate the database at the block level
The Schema Conversion Tool, to convert schema, views, and stored procedures ahead of the DMS data migration
Migration Hub, which automatically rewrites stored procedures to match the target engine

scenes.narration: Here's why. The sixty-day deadline eliminates a full refactor regardless of how attractive it looks — rehosting now via MGN guarantees the exit, and refactoring specific components afterward still captures the modernization goal, just on a timeline that can actually absorb it. And on the database question: DMS moves and replicates data, but it never rewrites schema or stored procedures written in a different engine's dialect. Because the source and target engines differ here, that's a heterogeneous migration, and the Schema Conversion Tool has to run first — converting what it safely can and flagging the rest for manual rework before DMS ever starts replicating.

answers.prompt: 60-day deadline, 500 servers, a colleague pushing for a full refactor.
answers.correct: Rehost via Application Migration Service now; schedule refactor work for specific components afterward.
answers.rationale: Sixty days is a hard, stated constraint that a multi-month-to-multi-year redesign cannot fit inside safely. Rehosting now guarantees the exit deadline; refactoring specific components afterward still captures the modernization goal, on a timeline that can actually absorb it.

answers.prompt: DMS alone, moving to a different database engine.
answers.correct: The Schema Conversion Tool must run first, converting schema, views, and stored procedures.
answers.rationale: DMS moves and replicates data — it doesn't rewrite schema or procedural code written for a different engine's dialect. Because source and target differ here, that's heterogeneous, and SCT converts what it safely can before DMS starts replicating, flagging anything that needs manual rework.

scenes.narration: Five things to carry forward. Know all seven Rs by name — retire, retain, rehost, replatform, repurchase, refactor, and relocate — because the exam loves blurring two of these together on purpose. Read the constraint first, then pick the R, then reach for the tool, never the reverse. The instant a scenario states a hard deadline or a limited skill set, refactor is very likely eliminated, no matter how attractive it looks. Application Migration Service executes rehost. Database Migration Service, plus the Schema Conversion Tool for different engines, executes replatform and database migration. Migration Hub tracks a multi-wave program — it never executes a migration itself, and mixing these three up is the single most common wrong-answer pattern in this domain. And when the network genuinely can't move the data in time, a physical transfer device wins — that crossover is something you compute, not something you guess. Next: chapter nineteen moves from getting workloads onto AWS to securing them once they're there — encryption key management, Secrets Manager, and GuardDuty's automated threat response.

props.heading: What to remember from this chapter
takeaways: Know all seven Rs by name: Retire, Retain, Rehost, Replatform, Repurchase, Refactor, Relocate — the exam blurs two together on purpose.
Constraint → R → Tool, never the reverse — a stated deadline or limited budget usually eliminates Refactor no matter how attractive it looks.
MGN executes Rehost. DMS, plus SCT for heterogeneous engines, executes Replatform and database migration. Migration Hub only tracks — it never executes.
Server Migration Service (SMS) is legacy — Application Migration Service (MGN) is the current rehost answer.
When the network can't move the data in time, a physical transfer device wins — that's a computed crossover, not a guess.

scenes.narration: Before you move on, work this through yourself. A retailer's ninety-server e-commerce platform must exit its current host in forty-five days. Leadership also wants the checkout flow rebuilt as serverless microservices while they're at it. Using this chapter's framework, what's your recommendation, and what happens to the serverless rebuild? There's a numeric, non-negotiable fact in that sentence, and there's a wish — the framework only works once you tell those two apart.
